rewrites.summary:
Iowa enacted a public-facility-use law in 2023 and bans state-funded gender-affirming care for minors; a September 2026 status check confirmed both remain in force, while the Iowa Supreme Court struck down the parallel ban on surgery coverage for adults — a partial carve-back.

An independent July 2026 legal-risk assessment lists Iowa among its 'worst states' group for transgender adults.

Independent analysts of the same period caution that legal-risk grades predict how the state behaves toward trans people, not how residents do, and that recorded violence counts are undercount floors.

rewrites.summary:
Florida's 2023 law (Fla. Stat. 553.865) makes it a second-degree criminal trespass — up to 60 days — to remain in a public bathroom or changing facility that does not match sex assigned at birth after a government employee orders departure; the ACLU of Florida calls it 'complex, confusing, and vague' and of limited actual coverage, and among at least 14 states with facility restrictions only Florida and Utah criminalise the act itself.

In March 2025 a 20-year-old trans student was arrested using a women's restroom in the State Capitol — believed the first arrest anywhere under a state bathroom ban. A Leon County judge dismissed the charge in June 2025 on speedy-trial grounds after the state missed a 90-day filing deadline; because the arrest was booked as trespass, the ban's constitutionality was never reached. Equality Florida and the Human Rights Campaign have issued named travel advisories warning of risks to trans travellers and movers.

Physical safety is comparatively better than the law suggests: a July 2026 analysis puts Florida's recorded killing rate for trans women at 3.7 per 100k per year, below the average of the worst-law states — itself an undercount floor.
rewrites.blindSummary: A 2023 state law makes remaining in a public bathroom or changing facility inconsistent with sex assigned at birth, after a government employee's instruction to leave, a criminal trespass (second-degree misdemeanour, up to 60 days); of at least 14 states with facility restrictions, only this state and one other criminalise the act itself, and the state's civil-liberties union calls the law complex and vague. The first arrest believed anywhere under such a law occurred in a seat-of-government women's restroom (March 2025); the charge was dismissed on speedy-trial grounds before the ban's constitutionality could be challenged, and both a state and the nation's largest LGBTQ organisation issued named travel advisories. Recorded killings of trans women run 3.7 per 100k per year, below the worst-law-state average.

An April 2025 wire report: the first arrest believed anywhere under a state transgender bathroom criminal ban, in a seat-of-government women's restroom; second-degree trespass, up to 60 days; only two states criminalise the act itself.

A July 2025 legal-news report: the trespass charge was dismissed on speedy-trial grounds after prosecutors missed a 90-day filing deadline; the trespass booking barred constitutional challenge to the ban itself.
An April 2023 press release issuing one of the country's only named state-level LGBTQ travel advisories; the nation's largest LGBTQ advocacy group joined with an updated advisory in 2024.

A July 2026 data analysis overlaying legal-risk grades on recorded trans-homicide counts: this state's rate (3.7 per 100k/yr) is below the worst-law-state average; all counts are acknowledged floors from an undercounted project.

rewrites.summary:
Montana has passed laws that would grade among the country's worst — including a facility-use ban and a public-buildings bathroom ban — but state courts have repeatedly blocked or enjoined them under the state constitution, leaving little of the anti-trans statutory book in force.

That makes Montana the anomaly of the 2026 legal-risk assessments: the only state whose risk grade was lowered — from 'worst laws' to 'high risk' — by cumulative court rulings and injunctions, in the February 2026 cycle. Statutory risk is high; enforcement risk is genuinely mixed.

It is the only state whose risk grade was lowered — worst-law group to high-risk — by cumulative court rulings in a February 2026 assessment; statutory risk is high, enforcement risk mixed.
blindSourceSummaries: An independent national legal-risk map (July 2026 update, republished by a news aggregator): this state is the flagged anomaly — worst-grade laws repeatedly blocked by state courts, sitting a tier below the worst group; the same update moves another state to the harshest tier.

The newsletter edition of the same legal-risk map, February 2026 cycle: this state's downgrade from worst-laws to high-risk is recorded as the only court-driven improvement ever, with most of the anti-trans statute book enjoined; other states escalated in the same cycle.
rewrites.notes: Dropped 'pride-flag ban'/HB121 clause (absent from both audited sources); kept court-blocked improvement and grade change, both source-backed.

rewrites.summary:
A July 2026 data analysis places Georgia's recorded killing rate for trans women at 4.8 per 100k per year — among the country's highest — and a Georgia law-review article documents the long-run fatality concentration around Atlanta: at least 15 fatal cases statewide across 1990–2014 (11 in Atlanta) and 16 more across 2015–2023 (8 in Atlanta). Both series are treated by their authors as undercount floors.

The same analysis's warning applies to Georgia directly: its legal-risk grade describes how the state behaves, not how its people do — here a jurisdiction whose documented danger to trans people has been violence on the street more than legislation from the legislature.

rewrites.summary:
A July 2026 national legal-risk assessment places Arizona among its 'low-risk states' group: it has largely refrained from targeting transgender adults, and although it has enacted policies affecting trans youth, the map's author considers them unlikely to be extended to adults. That is the assessment's praise of restraint, not of protection — no extraordinary protective measures are recorded for Arizona.

The local scene has tracked the national chill: Tucson cancelled its historic 2026 Pride celebration, citing a political and financial environment that made hosting nearly impossible and attending potentially unsafe.
